title: Trump overhauls campaign team, readies long-delayed TV ads
text: Donald Trump is resetting his 2016 campaign: he is getting ready to launch his first round of general election television ads in four crucial battleground states after reshuffling the top ranks of his team in an effort to sharpen his message and recover ground lost to Hillary Clinton in the polls. “I am committed to doing whatever it takes to win this election, and ultimately become President because our country cannot afford four more years of the failed Obama-Clinton policies which have endangered our financial and physical security,” the Republican nominee said in a statement released early Wednesday that announced the newest staffing changes. In a move characterized as an expansion, Trump elevated pollster Kellyanne Conway to campaign manager and appointed Stephen Bannon, co-founder of Breitbart News, as the campaign's chief executive. According to the statement, Paul Manafort, who took charge after Corey Lewandowski left in June, will keep his current title and work closely with Conway and Bannon as the campaign moves forward. Separately, a senior Trump aide told Fox News that the campaign will begin running TV ads on Friday in the battleground states of Ohio, Pennsylvania, Florida and North Carolina. That would be three days ahead of the schedule Manafort originally set; the campaign had been planning to start its ads after the Olympics, which finish on Sunday. Clinton, by contrast, has been saturating the airwaves with ads while opening up a significant post-convention lead in a number of battleground and national polls. Trump appears to be shifting his approach amid concerns that his off-the-cuff style may be damaging him in the general election environment.

title: U.S. pledges additional $364 million in humanitarian aid for Syrians
text: The U.S. State Department announced on Tuesday that it was giving an additional $364 million in humanitarian assistance to help Syrians caught up in the country’s civil war, raising total U.S. humanitarian spending on Syria to about $5.9 billion. Anne Richard, Assistant Secretary of State for Population, Refugees and Migration, said the money would help supply food, shelter, safe drinking water, medical care and other support to millions of Syrian refugees and the communities hosting them. Speaking at a State Department briefing, Richard said roughly three-quarters of the new funding would go to people still inside Syria, with the remainder assisting Syrians who have left the country. She also said the United States had admitted some 85,000 refugees in the past fiscal year, which ends Sept. 30. Of those, about 12,500 were Syrian refugees, more than the administration’s target of 10,000, she said. State Department spokesman Mark Toner said the drive for more humanitarian aid funding came partly in response to worsening conditions in Aleppo following the collapse of a ceasefire sponsored by the United States and Russia. Forces loyal to Syrian President Bashar al-Assad have launched a massive offensive against rebel-held areas of the city, where some 250,000 civilians are thought to be trapped. Intense bombing has killed hundreds of people, many of them in buildings brought down by bunker-buster bombs. “Until the past few weeks we felt like we were on a firm path towards a possible diplomatic resolution to this. We still believe that’s possible,” Toner told a briefing. “That doesn’t mean we’re not mindful ... of the tremendous humanitarian suffering that’s going on right now in Aleppo. And that’s why we’re working so hard to ramp up our assistance,” he added.

title: Cities and counties urge court to lift block on Obama immigration programs
text: Leaders of more than 70 cities and counties, some of them breaking with their own states, signed on to a legal brief filed Monday that asks an appeals court to let President Barack Obama's deportation relief policies go ahead. "Continuing to delay implementation of the president’s executive action on immigration hurts our economy and puts families at risk," New York Mayor Bill de Blasio (D) said in a statement. De Blasio led the effort together with Los Angeles Mayor Eric Garcetti (D) as part of Cities United for Immigration Action. "Cities are where immigrants live, and cities are where the president's executive action will be successfully implemented," he went on. "Our cities are united, and we will fight for the immigration reform this nation needs and deserves -- whether in the courtroom, in Congress, or in our communities. Make no mistake about it: our voices will be heard." Under the policies Obama announced in November, as many as 5 million undocumented immigrants with longstanding ties to the U.S. could be allowed to stay and work temporarily. Twenty-six states, led by Texas, brought the lawsuit, arguing that the relief programs would harm them and violate the Constitution. They have won backing from some Republican members of Congress and governors. But 14 states and the District of Columbia, some of them led by Republicans, filed an amicus brief arguing that the programs should be allowed to proceed. Garcetti and de Blasio led a similar brief in January that drew about 30 signatures. The new brief is supported by mayors, county executives and governments from 73 cities and counties in 27 states. The National League of Cities and the U.S. Conference of Mayors have also signed on to the brief. According to the brief's organizers, the cities and counties are home to 43 million people.

title: U.S. and China fail to reach trade agreement, raising doubts on wider ties
text: The United States and China were unable on Wednesday to agree on major new measures to cut the U.S. trade deficit with China, raising doubts about President Donald Trump’s economic and security relationship with Beijing. The yearly economic dialogue in Washington closed with news conferences cancelled, no joint statement and no fresh announcements on U.S. access to the Chinese market. A senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak publicly, said the two sides had a “frank exchange” but could not agree on most of the major bilateral trade and economic issues that mattered to the United States. According to the official, these included U.S. demands for access to China’s financial services markets, cuts to excess Chinese steel capacity, lower auto tariffs, reduced subsidies for state-owned enterprises, an end to Chinese data localization requirements and the lifting of ownership caps on foreign firms in China. “China acknowledged our shared objective to reduce the trade deficit which both sides will work cooperatively to achieve,” U.S. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin and U.S. Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross said in a short statement, pointing to a rare area of agreement. The Chinese embassy in Washington presented the talks positively, saying in a statement that both sides had recognized “significant progress” on the 100-day talks and would work together to cut the trade deficit. “The two sides will expand areas of cooperation in services and increase trade in services; expand mutual investment, and create a more open, equitable, transparent and convenient investment environment,” the embassy said. Chinese Vice Finance Minister Zhu Guangyao said after the talks ended that both sides agreed one way to tackle the trade imbalance is for the United States to increase its exports to China, rather than reduce imports from China.

title: Former Georgian president Saakashvili forces his way across Ukraine border
text: Former Georgian president Mikheil Saakashvili and a crowd of his supporters pushed past guards to enter Ukraine from the Polish border on Sunday, ending a drawn-out standoff between Saakashvili and the Ukrainian authorities. To shouts of “victory” and “glory to Ukraine”, Saakashvili came back to Ukraine even though his one-time ally, Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko, had stripped him of Ukrainian citizenship, and despite facing possible arrest and deportation. Poroshenko had invited Saakashvili to serve as a regional governor and help push through reforms after protests in 2014 toppled a pro-Russian president in Kiev. But Saakashvili resigned as governor of Odessa in November, accusing Poroshenko of abetting corruption. Thousands of Saakashvili's supporters massed at the border on Sunday, while prominent lawmakers, among them former Ukrainian prime minister Yulia Tymoshenko, travelled with him from Poland. Saakashvili had attempted to cross by train, but the train never left its station in the Polish town of Przemysl. The woman in charge of the Ukrainian train said the authorities had ordered her - she would not say whether Polish or Ukrainian - to keep the train from leaving until Saakashvili got off. He then went to the border by bus and was stopped by guards who sealed off the area, creating a tailback of vehicles. Supporters forced their way through and escorted him across. “I came with my Ukrainian passport, I wanted to show my passport and make a statement,” a triumphant Saakashvili told supporters after crossing. “Instead, the authorities arranged this circus.” Poroshenko's spokesman did not respond to a request for comment. “The crowd broke through the Shehyni checkpoint,” Oleh Slobodyan, a spokesman for the Ukrainian border service, wrote on Facebook. “The fight started. It's hard to predict the consequences of this situation.”

title: Palestinian unity deal is falling apart, says Hamas leader in Gaza
text: The Gaza leader of the Palestinian Islamist group Hamas said on Thursday that a reconciliation agreement with President Mahmoud Abbas's Fatah faction was collapsing, only 10 weeks after it was reached. The rivals signed the Cairo-brokered deal on Oct. 12 after Hamas agreed to give up administrative control of the Gaza Strip, including its border crossings with Egypt and Israel, a decade after it seized the enclave in a civil war. The agreement closed a deep divide between Abbas's Western-backed mainstream Fatah and Hamas, an Islamist movement that Western countries and Israel designate as a terrorist group. But ongoing disputes have held up its implementation. Yehya Al-Sinwar, Hamas's chief in Gaza and one of the main architects of the unity deal, gave a gloomy assessment on Thursday, suggesting it could meet the same fate as many reconciliation efforts over the past decade. “The reconciliation project is falling apart. Only a blind man can't see that,” Sinwar said in comments published by pro-Hamas media. One of the most recent disputes arose earlier this month when, according to Fatah officials, Hamas missed a deadline to finish handing over Gaza to Abbas's West Bank-based government. Hamas says it has relinquished all administrative control in Gaza. Prime minister Rami Al-Hamdallah said Hamas had not transferred funds as agreed, while Hamas said Hamdallah's government had not paid salaries in Gaza as agreed. Sinwar has said in the past that his group would not return to governing Gaza and that he was committed to making the deal work. Fatah officials declined to comment immediately. “Reconciliation is collapsing because some people want to get from it the relinquishing of arms and the closing of tunnels,” Sinwar said without elaborating, but in apparent reference to Fatah.
